title: The Way of Devotion
intro: Ninety days through chapters 7 to 12 of the Bhagavad Gita, the heart of its teaching on devotion.

posts.caption: This plan follows the Bhagavad Gita through chapters 7 to 12, where Krishna, serving as the warrior Arjuna's charioteer on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, turns to the nature of God and to bhakti, loving devotion. Chapter 7 opens with a promise: knowledge (jñāna) together with vijñāna (Besant's 'wisdom'), so complete that nothing more remains to be known. Shankara takes vijñāna as realisation, knowing the truth by direct experience; Ramanuja, as knowing how God is distinct from everything else.

Krishna stresses how rare it is to know God fully. Among thousands of people, scarcely one strives for spiritual perfection, and among those who succeed, scarcely one knows him tattvataḥ, 'in essence', as he truly is. The rarity underlines the worth of the complete knowledge he has just promised to share.

Krishna begins explaining how he relates to the world. Everything material is his 'lower' nature, prakriti, in eight parts: the five elements (earth, water, fire, air, and ether or space), plus mind, intellect (buddhi, Besant's 'Reason') and ego (ahankara, 'Egoism'). The striking point, shared with Sankhya philosophy, is that mind and ego count as part of matter too. His 'higher' nature, he says next, is the life by which the universe is upheld.

posts.display: I the sapidity in waters, O son of Kuntî, I the radiance in moon and sun; the Word of Power in all the Vedas, sound in ether, and virility in men.
posts.caption: Krishna explains how he can be found in the everyday world: he is the essence of each thing, the taste in water (Besant's 'sapidity'), the light of sun and moon. In the Gita's teaching, this means God is not only far away but present in what makes each thing what it is. The 'Word of Power' is the pranava, the sacred syllable Om, present in all the Vedas.

The list continues: Krishna is the pure fragrance of the earth, the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings and the austerity (tapas) of ascetics. As commentators explain, each entry names the quality that makes a thing what it is, and Krishna is that core. The pairings follow classical Indian philosophy, which links each element to a sense: taste with water, sound with space, scent with earth.

Krishna calls himself the eternal seed (bīja) of all beings, the source from which everything grows. He is also the intelligence of the intelligent and the splendour of the splendid. The point is that the Gita treats whatever is finest in a person, their insight or their brilliance, as a sign of God at work in them. The phrase tejas tejasvinām aham returns word for word in chapter 10.

The Gita does not condemn all desire. Krishna is the strength of the strong when it is free of craving, and he is desire itself when it is not contrary to dharma, the right order of things (Besant's 'duty'). Commentators read this as desire kept within ethical bounds; Shankara's example is the wish for food and drink that sustains the body.

Krishna names what keeps people from seeing him: his māyā, which Besant translates 'illusion', the divine power that veils reality, woven from the three guṇas, the qualities of nature. It is hard to cross, he says, but those who take refuge in him cross over it. In the Gita's teaching, the way past this veil is surrender. The verb for it, prapad-, gives prapatti, a central idea in Ramanuja's tradition.

Krishna acknowledges that people turn to God for very different reasons: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the one seeking some gain, and the wise (jñānī). Strikingly, he calls all four virtuous, and two verses later, noble. The point is that even prayer born of trouble or need counts as a real beginning, though he singles out the wise, whose devotion is undivided, as dearest to him.

Krishna describes where the long path of wisdom leads: after many births, the wise come to him, seeing that 'Vāsudeva is all'. Vāsudeva, 'son of Vasudeva', is a name of Krishna. The verse treats this vision of God in everything as the fruit of many lifetimes, and such a mahātmā, 'great soul', as very rare. Advaita reads it as non-duality; Vaishnava schools, as everything depending on God.

Krishna speaks of people who worship other deities. Whatever form a devotee chooses to worship with faith (śraddhā), he says, he himself makes that faith steady. The verse is often cited for the Gita's breadth, though the verses that follow rank such worship below devotion to Krishna himself.

Krishna's knowledge spans all beings, past, present and yet to come, while he himself remains unknown to them. The verse just before gives the reason: his yoga-māyā, his creative power, veils him from the world. The theme of a God who knows all but is hard to know runs through these chapters.

Krishna explains why beings fail to know him: from birth they are caught in the pull of desire and the push of aversion. These give rise to the 'pairs of opposites' (dvandva), such as pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour, which keep the mind swinging back and forth. Rising above them marks the steady sage of chapter 2. Bhārata and Parantapa ('scorcher of foes') are names for Arjuna.

Chapter 7 closes by linking devotion and knowledge: those who take refuge in Krishna while striving for freedom from old age and death (jarā-maraṇa; Besant has 'birth and death') come to know the whole truth. That includes Brahman, the Eternal, adhyātma, the Self, and karma, action. These terms, and three more in the next verse, prompt Arjuna's questions at the start of chapter 8.

Chapter 8 begins with Arjuna asking how Krishna is known at the time of death. Krishna answers that whoever leaves the body remembering him at the end enters his being, without doubt. The point is that the last thought matters, a teaching reflected in the custom, in many Hindu families, of reciting God's name at a deathbed. It is the Gita's main teaching on the moment of death.

The principle behind the previous verse: whatever a person dwells on when leaving the body, they go to that state, because it is what they have been absorbed in all along. The Bhagavata Purana tells of King Bharata, who in his final moments thought of a pet deer and was reborn as one.

So Krishna gives Arjuna a twofold instruction: remember him at all times, and fight. Remembrance of the divine is meant to go along with Arjuna's duty as a warrior, not replace it. Readers range from those who take the battle literally to those, like Gandhi, who read it as an allegory of the inner struggle.

How can anyone be sure to remember God at the end? Krishna's answer is practice (abhyāsa): a mind trained by constant effort not to wander, meditating on the supreme divine Person (puruṣa). The point is that the last thought grows out of a lifetime of habit. Abhyāsa is the same word Krishna used in chapter 6 for taming the restless mind.

posts.display: "Aum!" the one syllabled Eternal, reciting, thinking upon Me, he who goeth forth, abandoning the body, he goeth on the highest path.
posts.caption: Krishna describes the death of a practised yogi: senses withdrawn, breath drawn up, chanting Om while remembering him. Om is the single sacred syllable that the Upanishads identify with Brahman, the Eternal, so sounding it turns the whole self toward the highest at the last moment. Besant spells it 'Aum', reflecting its three sounds, a, u and m, which the Mandukya Upanishad explains at length.

After describing the demanding yogic death, Krishna offers something simpler: to one who remembers him constantly, thinking of nothing else, he is easily reached (sulabha). The verse shifts the weight from yogic technique to steady, loving remembrance. That theme grows through the coming chapters as bhakti, devotion.

Krishna says the great souls (mahātmās) who reach him are not born again into this impermanent world of sorrow. Release from saṁsāra, the cycle of birth and death, is called moksha, liberation, the goal the Gita points toward throughout.

Krishna widens the view to cosmic time: a single day of Brahmā, the creator, lasts a thousand yugas (ages), and his night as long. In later Puranic reckoning that day comes to 4.32 billion human years. The point, made in the verse just before, is that even worlds that last so long come and go; only reaching Krishna is beyond return. Carl Sagan remarked on these timescales in his 1980 series Cosmos.

At the dawn of Brahmā's day, all manifest things stream out of the unmanifest (avyakta); at nightfall they dissolve back into it. The Gita pictures the universe as cyclical, endlessly emerging and withdrawing, rather than created once and ending once.

Beyond the endless cycles of creation and dissolution, Krishna says, there is something that never perishes. He calls it the unmanifest and imperishable (akṣara), the highest goal and his own supreme abode (dhāma). Those who reach it do not return to the round of birth. The point is that the goal is not a better place within the cycle but a way out of it.

That supreme Person (puruṣa), in whom all beings dwell and by whom everything is pervaded, is reached by bhakti that is ananya, 'with no other' object. Undivided devotion, ananya bhakti, recurs through chapters 8 to 11 and becomes central to chapter 12.

Krishna sums up an old Vedic teaching on two paths a soul may take at death. The bright path, linked with fire, day and the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa), leads beyond rebirth; the dark path, linked with smoke and night, leads back to it. Some readers also take light and darkness as knowledge and ignorance. In the Mahabharata, the wounded Bhishma waits on his bed of arrows for uttarāyaṇa before he dies.

Chapter 8 ends by saying that the yogi who knows these teachings goes beyond all the merit promised for Vedic study, sacrifice, austerity and charity, and reaches the supreme, primal abode. The Gita often honours ritual merit while pointing past it to something higher.

Chapter 9 is called the Yoga of the Royal Knowledge and Royal Secret, after Krishna's praise of this teaching in its opening verses. Here he warns that it bears fruit only with śraddhā, faith or trust: without it, people do not reach him and return to saṁsāra, the round of death and rebirth. The point is that this knowledge is not just learned; it has to be taken to heart.

Krishna describes a paradox. In his unmanifest form he pervades the whole universe, and all beings rest in him, yet he does not rest in them. Commentators read this as saying that God supports the world without being limited or changed by it.

Krishna gives an image for the paradox: the mighty wind moves everywhere, yet always within ākāśa, space (Besant's 'Ether'). Space holds the wind without being disturbed by it, just as all beings rest in Krishna without binding him.

Krishna returns to the cosmic cycles of chapter 8. At the end of a kalpa, a world-age, all beings pass back into his prakriti, his nature; at the start of the next he sends them forth again. In this picture creation is not a single event but a rhythm repeated again and again.

Krishna explains how he can be the source of the world without being caught up in it. Prakriti, nature, brings forth everything moving and unmoving, while he presides as adhyakṣa, the overseer. The verse before describes him as seated apart, unbound by all this activity. Chapter 4 draws the lesson: whoever understands how God acts without being bound is not bound by action either.

posts.display: The foolish disregard Me, when clad in human semblance, ignorant of My supreme nature, the great Lord of beings.
posts.caption: Krishna says the deluded disregard him because he has taken a human form, not knowing his supreme nature as the great Lord of beings. To Arjuna, Krishna is also a friend, a cousin and his charioteer, a tension that comes to a head in chapter 11.

In contrast to those who disregard him, Krishna describes the mahātmās, 'great souls', who take shelter in his divine nature (daivī prakṛti). Knowing him as the imperishable source of beings, they worship him with minds turned to nothing else. The contrast between divine and demonic natures returns at length in chapter 16.

Krishna describes those who offer the 'sacrifice of knowledge' (jñāna-yajña), worshipping him as the One, as distinct, and in his many forms facing every direction. Shankara takes the first as worship through realising that the supreme Brahman is one. The verse is often cited for the Gita's openness to more than one way of approaching God.

posts.display: I the Father of this universe, the Mother, the Supporter, the Grandsire, the Holy one to be known, the Word of Power, and also the Rik, Sâma, and Yajur.
posts.caption: In a litany that runs over several verses, Krishna names himself father, mother, sustainer and grandsire of the universe, the holy one to be known, Om (the 'Word of Power') and the Vedas themselves. The images join closeness and holiness: God is as near as a parent and as sacred as scripture. The Gita, like many older texts, names three Vedas; the Atharva came to be counted as a fourth.

The litany ends with pairs of opposites. Krishna gives heat, holds back the rain and releases it; he is immortality and death, being and non-being (sat and asat). Commentators read sat and asat in various ways, for instance as the manifest world and its unmanifest cause. Either way, the verse places both sides of each pair within the divine.

One of the Gita's most quoted lines is a promise of care. To those who worship him with undivided minds, always devoted, Krishna says he carries their yoga-kṣema, often explained as securing what they lack and protecting what they have. For devotees, it is an assurance that God looks after those who rely on him. The phrase yogakṣemaṁ vahāmyaham is the motto of the Life Insurance Corporation of India.

Krishna says that even devotees of other deities (devas, Besant's 'Shining Ones') who worship with faith are really worshipping him, though not in the prescribed way. The verse is often cited for the Gita's inclusiveness, while traditions differ over how far such worship falls short.

Krishna turns ordinary life into worship: whatever Arjuna does, eats, offers, gives or undertakes as austerity is to be done as an offering to Krishna. The verse links the devotion of chapter 9 to the karma yoga, the yoga of action, taught earlier in the Gita.

Krishna says he is the same to all beings, with no one hateful to him and no one favoured. Yet those who worship him with devotion are in him, and he in them. Shankara compares this to a fire, which keeps the cold away from those who come near it without favouring anyone.

Even the worst wrongdoer who worships Krishna with undivided devotion is to be counted good, he says, for that person has resolved rightly, and soon becomes righteous and finds lasting peace. The closing words, na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati, are often quoted. Krishna asks Arjuna to declare them (pratijānīhi), which Besant renders 'know thou for certain'.
posts.display: Even if the most sinful worship Me, with undivided heart, he too must be accounted righteous, for he hath rightly resolved. Speedily he becometh dutiful and goeth to eternal peace; O Kaunteya, know thou for certain that My devotee perisheth never.
On Me fix thy mind, be devoted to Me; sacrifice to Me; prostrate thyself before Me; harmonised thus in the Self, thou shalt come unto Me, having Me as thy supreme goal.
posts.caption: Chapter 9 closes with Krishna's call to Arjuna in four parts: mind fixed on him, devoted to him, worshipping him and bowing to him, with Krishna as the supreme goal. Many teachers treat it as a summary of bhakti, a devotion that takes in thought, feeling and action alike. The first line returns word for word in 18:65, near the end of the Gita.

Chapter 10 is the Vibhūti Yoga, the Yoga of Divine Glories. Krishna opens by offering to speak again for Arjuna's good, to a listener Besant calls beloved; the Sanskrit can also mean one who delights in hearing. The chapter grows into a long list of the forms in which the divine can be recognised in the world.

Krishna says that whoever knows him as unborn and beginningless, the great Lord of the worlds, is free of delusion and released from all wrongdoing. Just before, he said that even the gods and great sages do not know his origin, since he is the origin of them all.

posts.display: Reason, wisdom, non-illusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, calmness, pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, fear, and also courage, harmlessness, equanimity, content, austerity, almsgiving, fame and obloquy are the various characteristics of beings issuing from Me.
posts.caption: Krishna lists the qualities of living beings, pleasant and painful alike: understanding, forgiveness, truth, calm, fear and courage, fame and disgrace. All of them, he says, come from him alone. The list includes ahiṁsā, non-harm (Besant's 'harmlessness'), a value later central to Gandhi's thought.

Krishna describes what devotion looks like among his devotees: minds absorbed in him, lives given to him, enlightening one another and always speaking of him, they find contentment and joy. The picture is of devotion as something shared and joyful, not solitary or grim. In the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition, verses 10:8 to 10:11 are often singled out as four verses that sum up the whole Gita.

posts.display: Arjuna said: Thou art the supreme Eternal, the supreme Abode, the supreme Purity, eternal divine man, primeval Deity, unborn, the Lord!
posts.caption: Arjuna responds with praise, calling Krishna the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the eternal divine Person (puruṣa), the first of the gods, unborn and all-pervading. It is one of the Gita's clearest statements of who Arjuna now takes his friend and charioteer to be.

Arjuna tells Krishna that only he knows himself, by himself. The point is a humble one: no one else, not even gods or sages, can fully grasp God, which is why Arjuna goes on to ask Krishna to describe his own glories. He piles up titles: source of beings, lord of beings, god of gods, ruler of the world. Puruṣottama, 'Supreme Person', became one of Krishna's best-known names.

Krishna agrees to describe his divine glories (vibhūtis), but only the chief ones, since there is no end to them. What follows is a long catalogue, verse after verse, naming the best in each class of things: of rivers, of mountains, of sages, of warriors.

In this catalogue Krishna names the finest member of each group as a way of pointing to himself. Among the Vedas he is the Sama Veda, the Veda of sung chants; among the gods, Vāsava, a name of Indra, their king; among the senses, the mind that directs them; and in living beings, consciousness (cetanā). The point is that the divine shows itself most clearly in what is best or most central.

Krishna keeps naming the best of each kind: among great sages, Bhṛgu; among words, the single syllable Om; among offerings, japa, the quiet repetition of a sacred name or mantra; among immovable things, the Himalaya. Many commentators explain japa's first place by its purity: it needs no outward materials and harms no living being. Japa, often counted on a string of beads, remains one of the most widespread Hindu devotional practices.

Each entry in Krishna's catalogue is the greatest of its kind, a window onto the divine. Among purifiers he is the wind; among warriors, Rāma, usually understood as the hero of the Ramayana and himself honoured as an avatar of Vishnu. Among water creatures he is the makara, often identified with the crocodile, and among rivers the Ganga, here called Jāhnavī after the sage Jahnu, who in a well-known story swallowed the river and released it.

Krishna is the beginning, middle and end of all creation. Among branches of learning he is knowledge of the Self (adhyātma-vidyā), which commentators rank highest because it leads to liberation. Among those who argue, he is vāda, which Shankara explains as discussion aimed at finding the truth, unlike argument aimed only at winning. The divine, in other words, is in honest inquiry, not in point-scoring.

A startling entry: Krishna is the gambling of cheats, alongside splendour, victory, resolve and the goodness of the good. Commentators read it as Krishna being the most potent thing in every class, even a dark one. In the Mahabharata, a rigged dice game cost the Pandavas their kingdom, setting off the events that led to this war.

Krishna's catalogue reaches into public life. Among those who govern, he is the rod of authority (daṇḍa, Besant's 'sceptre'), the power to restrain wrongdoing; among those seeking victory, sound policy (nīti); among secrets, silence; and the knowledge of the wise. The point is that the divine is found in statecraft and strategy as well as in temples and sages. Classical Indian texts call the science of government daṇḍanīti.

Krishna sums up the catalogue: whatever is glorious, beautiful or mighty arises from a mere fragment (aṁśa) of his splendour. The long list works less as an inventory than as a way of seeing, in which excellence anywhere points to the divine.

Chapter 10 closes with Krishna setting the details aside: he upholds this entire universe with a single fragment of himself, and remains. The idea that the cosmos is only a part of the divine echoes the Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta, where all beings are a quarter of the cosmic Person.

Chapter 11, the Vision of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa Darśana), is the dramatic peak of the Gita. It opens with Arjuna saying that Krishna's teaching on the Self has taken away his confusion. Out of that new confidence comes a bold request.

Arjuna asks to see Krishna's aiśvara rūpa, his form as the sovereign Lord. Having heard about the divine glories, he now wants to see them. He addresses Krishna as Parameśvara, 'supreme Lord', and Puruṣottama, 'supreme Person'.

Krishna agrees and tells Arjuna to behold his forms, by the hundreds and thousands, divine and of many colours and shapes. Over the next verses he points out the gods of the Vedic world within his body. The Sanskrit rūpāṇi is plural: not one image but countless forms at once.

Krishna invites Arjuna to see the whole universe, everything moving and unmoving, gathered in one place within his body, along with anything else he wishes to see. Gudākeśa, an epithet of Arjuna, is often explained as 'conqueror of sleep'. In the next verse Krishna explains that ordinary eyes will not be enough.

Ordinary eyes cannot see this form, so Krishna grants Arjuna a divya cakṣu, a 'divine eye'. The point, as many commentators read it, is that God is not seen by human senses or effort alone; the vision is a gift. The narrator Sanjaya has a similar gift: in the Mahabharata, the sage Vyasa gives him divine sight so he can describe the battle to the blind king Dhritarashtra.

Sanjaya, the narrator relaying the battlefield to the blind king Dhritarashtra, reaches for a comparison: if the light of a thousand suns blazed up at once in the sky, it might resemble the radiance of that great being (mahātman). The point is that what Arjuna sees outshines anything in ordinary experience. It is among the best-known images in the Gita.

Arjuna, overwhelmed, begins a long hymn. Within Krishna's body he sees all the gods, every kind of being, Brahmā the creator on his lotus, the sages and the divine serpents. The point is that even the gods are contained within the one Lord. Here the Sanskrit shifts to the longer triṣṭubh metre, and Besant switches to English blank verse to match.

Arjuna names what he sees: the imperishable, the supreme one to be known, the final resting place of the universe, and the guardian of eternal dharma. He calls Krishna the eternal Person. The word for 'eternal' here, sanātana, is the one in Sanatana Dharma, a name many Hindus use for their tradition.

The vision turns frightening. Krishna's form touches the sky, blazing in many colours, with gaping mouths and vast fiery eyes, and Arjuna confesses he has lost all steadiness and peace. The Gita does not soften the divine here: the God who is Arjuna's friend is also overwhelming and terrifying. Arjuna calls him Vishnu, reflecting the tradition that identifies the two.

Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies rushing into Krishna's flaming mouths, as rivers race toward the ocean. The next verse adds a second image, moths flying into a flame. The vision shows Arjuna what is about to happen on the field as if it had already happened.

posts.display: Reveal Thy Self; what awful Form art Thou? I worship Thee! Have mercy, God supreme! Thine inner Being I am fain to know; This Thy forth-streaming Life bewilders me.
posts.caption: Terrified, Arjuna asks the being before him who he is, bows, and begs for mercy. He wants to understand this primal one, because he cannot make sense of what the form is doing. Krishna's answer, in the next verse, is one of the most famous lines of the Gita.

posts.display_original: कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः । ऋतेऽपि त्वां न भविष्यन्ति सर्वे येऽवस्थिताः प्रत्यनीकेषु योधाः
posts.caption: Krishna answers that he is kāla, Time, grown mighty to destroy the worlds, and that the warriors ranged on both sides are already doomed. Kāla can also mean death. J. Robert Oppenheimer, who had studied Sanskrit, said in a 1965 television documentary that after the first atomic test in 1945 he remembered a version of this line: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.'

Krishna tells Arjuna to rise and win glory, since these warriors are already slain by him; Arjuna is to be only the nimitta-mātra, the mere instrument. Savyasācin, 'left-handed one', names Arjuna as an archer who can shoot with either hand. Readers differ on whether the passage concerns this battle or the soul's inner struggle.

Arjuna bows to Krishna from every side, before and behind, and calls him the All, since Krishna pervades everything. Advaita readers take this as pointing to non-duality; Ramanuja's school reads it as God dwelling in all things as their inner Self, the world being, in its terms, his body.

Arjuna remembers how casually he has treated Krishna: calling him friend, joking with him, sharing meals and rest, alone or in company. Now, having seen who Krishna is, he asks forgiveness for any disrespect. The scene holds together intimacy and awe, two poles of devotion.

posts.display: I have seen that which none hath seen before, My heart is glad, yet faileth me for fear; Show me, O God, Thine other Form again— Mercy, O God of Gods, home of all worlds.
posts.caption: Arjuna is thrilled and terrified at once, having seen what no one has seen before. He asks Krishna to show his other form again and to have mercy, calling him God of gods and dwelling place of the worlds (jagan-nivāsa). In the next verse he asks for the familiar four-armed form, with crown, mace and discus.

After returning to his gentle human form, Krishna explains that this vision cannot be won by Vedic study, sacrifice, charity or austerity. Only by bhakti that is ananya, devotion with no other object, can he be known, seen as he is and entered into. The verse is the hinge between chapter 11's vision and chapter 12's teaching on devotion.

Chapter 11 closes with a verse that gathers up its teaching: work done for Krishna, Krishna as the highest goal, devotion, freedom from attachment, and enmity toward no being. Shankara's commentary presents it as the essence of the whole Gita. The last quality, nirvaira, 'without enmity', stands out after a chapter about war.

posts.display: They who worship the Indestructible, the Ineffable, the unmanifested, Omnipresent, and Unthinkable, the Unchanging, Immutable, Eternal, restraining and subduing the senses, regarding everything equally, in the welfare of all rejoicing, these also come unto Me.
posts.caption: Chapter 12, Bhakti Yoga, opens with Arjuna asking which is better: devotion to Krishna in personal form, or meditation on the imperishable, unmanifest absolute. Krishna first calls his devotees the most accomplished in yoga, then adds that those who worship the formless, with senses restrained and rejoicing in the welfare of all, also reach him.

Krishna says the path of the unmanifest is harder, because embodied beings struggle to fix the mind on what has no form. Shankara reads this as a point about difficulty rather than worth; devotional schools take it as confirming that devotion to the personal God is the better path. The question remains a living one between traditions.

posts.display: Those verily who, renouncing all actions in Me and intent on Me, worship meditating on Me, with whole-hearted yoga, these I speedily lift up from the ocean of death and existence, O Pârtha, their minds being fixed on Me.
posts.caption: To those who offer all their actions to him and meditate on him with undivided devotion, Krishna promises to be their deliverer, swiftly lifting them out of the sea of saṁsāra, the cycle of birth and death. The image of saṁsāra as an ocean to be crossed is shared by Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions.

Krishna begins a graded series of paths. The first and highest: mind and intellect (buddhi) set wholly on him, so that Arjuna will dwell in him from then on. The verses that follow offer gentler steps, one after another, for anyone who finds this one too hard.

If the mind cannot yet rest steadily on Krishna, the next step is abhyāsa-yoga, the yoga of practice: returning to him again and again. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras likewise pair practice (abhyāsa) with non-attachment (vairāgya) as the way to still the mind.

If even steady practice is too hard, the next step is to make Krishna's work one's highest aim, doing actions for his sake. Even that, he says, leads to perfection (siddhi). In the verse after this, Krishna offers one more step.

The last and most accessible step: if even working for Krishna's sake is beyond reach, Arjuna can take refuge in him and give up the fruits of all his actions with self-control. Karma-phala-tyāga, renouncing the fruit of action, echoes the Gita's famous teaching in chapter 2 on acting without attachment to results.

Krishna ranks the paths: knowledge above practice, meditation above knowledge, and renouncing the fruits of action above meditation, for peace follows at once. Commentators explain in various ways why the simplest-seeming step is praised most. Gandhi, who called his own Gita translation Anasaktiyoga, 'the yoga of non-attachment', made this idea central.

posts.display: He who beareth no ill-will to any being, friendly and compassionate, without attachment and egoism, balanced in pleasure and pain, and forgiving, ever content, harmonious, with the self-controlled, resolute, with mind and Reason dedicated to Me, he, My devotee, is dear to Me.
posts.caption: Krishna now describes the devotee who is dear to him, in a portrait that runs to the end of the chapter. Such a person bears ill will to none, is friendly and compassionate, free of possessiveness and ego, even-minded in pleasure and pain, forgiving and content. The refrain 'dear to me' (me priyaḥ) closes verse after verse.

A two-way balance: the devotee neither troubles the world nor is troubled by it, and is free from the swings of elation, impatience, fear and agitation. The Sanskrit uses the same verb, udvij-, 'to be disturbed', in both directions.

This devotee expects nothing, is pure and capable, unconcerned and untroubled, and gives up every self-centred undertaking. Besant's 'expert' renders dakṣa, skilful or able, which suggests the Gita's ideal is clear, capable action without selfish motive rather than passivity.

The devotee dear to Krishna neither rejoices nor hates, grieves nor craves, and has given up both good and evil, śubha and aśubha. Commentators read that last phrase in different ways, from setting aside both merit and sin as binding, to letting go of attachment to pleasant and unpleasant results.

Praise and blame are alike to this devotee, who is quiet (maunī), content with whatever comes, and aniketa, literally 'without a fixed home'. Some take the word literally, of wandering renunciants; others read it as not being attached to any one place.

Chapter 12 ends, and this plan with it, with Krishna calling those who follow this nectar-like teaching of dharma with faith, holding him as their highest goal, exceedingly dear to him. Thank you for reading through the Gita's middle six chapters on devotion. The final six turn to the field and its knower, the three guṇas, and the meaning of true renunciation.
